text: Tally values from a small range, then print them in order.

When the values come from a small range (say 1 … 1000) but there are millions of them, tally them in a counting array (入门 4) and print each value as many times as it was seen. O(n + range), no comparisons at all (P1271).
Millions of numbers make input the bottleneck. With cin , turn on fast IO (fast in your template); never use endl per number.

text: The three O(n²) sorts, and what bubble sort counts.
Selection sort: for each position from the left, find the smallest value in the rest and swap it into place. It does at most n − 1 swaps but always about n²/2 comparisons, whatever the input.
Sort Comparisons Good for selection always ~n²/2 few swaps bubble up to ~n²/2 counting inversions insertion ~n to ~n²/2 nearly sorted data quick / std::sort ~n log n everything else
start pass 1 pass 2 pass 3

Bubble sort: walk the array, swapping neighbours that are out of order. After pass k the k largest values are in place at the end (green). Each swap fixes exactly one inversion (a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]).
So the number of bubble-sort swaps = the number of inversions = the minimum number of adjacent swaps needed to sort (P1116). O(n²): fine for n up to a few thousand.

Insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix and slides each new value into place: fast when the data is almost sorted. Selection sort repeatedly picks the minimum of the rest. All three are O(n²); use them to understand or to count, use sort to sort.
Partition around a pivot; k-th smallest; merge sort for comparison.
pivot 5: smaller to the left, bigger to the right
Quicksort: pick a pivot, move smaller values left and bigger values right (partition), then sort the two sides the same way. On average each level does O(n) work and there are about log n levels.
To find only the k-th smallest you need just one side after each partition: average O(n).
The standard library does this as nth_element .

Taking the first element as pivot makes already-sorted data O(n²). The middle element (or a random one) avoids that. Contest template problems (P1177) include such data on purpose; in practice just call sort .
After nth_element(a, a + k, a + n) , a[k] holds the value it would have after a full sort, everything before it is ≤ and everything after is ≥. Average O(n), faster than sorting (P1923).
With 5 × 106 numbers, slow input alone can time out: the two fast-IO lines are required here.

Merge sort sorts each half, then merges two sorted lists by repeatedly taking the smaller front value: always O(n log n). While merging, taking from the right half jumps over all values left in the left half, which counts inversions in O(n log n) instead of bubble sort's O(n²).
std::sort, sort-then-scan, and sorting records by several keys.
Order first, then many problems become a single scan.
sort(a, a + 5)
sort(a, a + n) puts a[0] … a[n-1] in increasing order in O(n log n). After sorting, equal values sit next to each other, the smallest is at the front, and the k-th smallest is at index k − 1.
The range is half-open: first element included, end pointer excluded. For a 1-based array use sort(a + 1, a + n + 1) .

After sorting, duplicates are neighbours and greedy choices are easy.
unique removes adjacent repeats, moving the kept values to the front and returning where they end; erase cuts off the rest. It only works after sort , which makes all copies adjacent (P1059).
Small value range? A marking array does the same: seen[x] = true , then print every marked value in order.
Jolly
Not jolly

Fewest items to reach a total: take the biggest first, which needs sorting in decreasing order (P2676). "Do the gaps cover 1 … n − 1 exactly?" is a marking array, or a sort of the gaps and a check that gap i equals i (P1152).
Main key first; each tie-break only when everything before it is equal.
Write the comparator as a ladder: compare key 1; if different, return that comparison.
Otherwise move to key 2, and so on. The last rung is usually the input order (an id you stored), which makes every order fully defined (P1093, P1068, P1786).

Need "same keys keep input order"? Either add the id as the last key, or call stable_sort , which never reorders equal elements (P1104: same birthday, later input first → id descending as the last key).
A comparator must be a strict order: cmp(x, x) must be false. Using >= or <= breaks sort , sometimes with a crash.
Cut-off lines: sort, take the score of the person at position ⌊m × 1.5⌋, then count everyone with score ≥ that line, because ties at the line all pass (P1068).
Numbers too long for long long can still be compared without big-number arithmetic: more digits means bigger; same length means dictionary order on the strings (P1781).
The same comparison works inside a sort comparator for big numbers kept as strings. 3D climbing (P5143) is a sort by height followed by summing distances between neighbours.

C C LANGUAGE · ADDITIONAL INFORMATION C sorts with qsort(base, count, size, cmp) from <stdlib.h> . The comparison receives two const void * pointers and returns a negative number, zero or a positive number, unlike C++'s true/false comparator.
Writing return x - y; can overflow for large values of opposite sign. (x > y) - (x < y) is safe.

Key points to memorise
1. sort(a, a + n) is O(n log n); 1-based: sort(a + 1, a + n + 1); decreasing: greater<int>().
2. After sorting: duplicates are adjacent, k-th smallest is at index k − 1.
3. Bubble-sort swaps = inversions = fewest adjacent swaps; O(n²).
4. Insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted data; still O(n²) in general.
5. Small value range: counting sort, O(n + range).
6. Quicksort: partition around a pivot; use the middle or a random pivot.
7. nth_element(a, a + k, a + n): k-th smallest in average O(n).
8. Merge sort is always O(n log n) and counts inversions while merging.
9. Remove duplicates: sort, then v.erase(unique(…), v.end()).
10. Multi-key comparator: a ladder of "if different, return"; finish with the id.
11. Comparator must be strict: never >=; stable_sort keeps equal items in input order.
12. Compare huge numbers as strings: length first, then dictionary order.
13. Millions of inputs: fast IO on, no endl.
14. (C) qsort uses a comparator returning negative / zero / positive.
